She was last seen at baseline about 6 hours prior. Three years prior, she had experienced a similar event requiring mechanical thrombectomy, with the cause remaining unknown. Medical history included well-controlled hypertension, obesity, migraines, and recurrent immune thrombocytopenia in childhood. Current medications were aspirin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. There was no pain, inflammation, fever, trauma, or history of ocular infection, and his overall health was unchanged. On examination, abduction of the right eye was restricted. There were no signs of proptosis, strabismus, visual impairment, or inflammation in either eye; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies, including an infectious work-up, were negative.

A 5‐year‐9‐month‐old, 170‐kg domestic llama mare was referred for a 1‐week history of dyspnea and inspiratory noise. The owner reported that an esophageal obstruction had been suspected by the referring veterinarian, but spasmolytics and passage of a gastric tube did not improve the signs. On presentation, the llama was bright, alert, in good condition (body‐condition score 3.5/5) with normal vital signs. In the middle third of the ventral cervical region, there was a 10 × 8 × 3‐cm subcutaneous mass that was partially firm and fluctuant, slightly painful, and mildly warm; the overlying skin appeared normal. No dysphagia, other masses, or lymphadenopathy were detected. A CBC showed mild leukocytosis (23,690/µL; reference 8,700–17,500/µL) with neutrophilia (92.4%; reference 42.4–76.4%) and lymphopenia (3.0%; reference 7.0–32.5%); eosinophils were decreased; hematocrit was 39.8% (reference 27.0–39.0%), MCV was mildly increased, and MCHC was mildly decreased. Flexible endoscopy of the esophagus and trachea under sedation revealed no abnormalities. Cervical ultrasonography showed a well‐demarcated, heterogeneously echogenic, encapsulated mass with no communication with the trachea or esophagus and no intrinsic vascular flow. Thoracic and cervical radiographs demonstrated a ventral soft‐tissue‐density mass in the mid‐to‐caudal cervical region causing a mild mass effect on the trachea; no pulmonary lesions or further abnormalities were noted.

clinical_record:
A 59-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a crusty lesion in the right fronto-orbital region present for several months. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was an irregularly shaped 5 × 3 cm plaque with multiple superficial crusts. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. 

An excisional biopsy of the lesion showed lobules and detached aggregates of eosinophilic keratinocytes with pleomorphic nuclei and prominent nucleoli infiltrating the reticular dermis; there was no clear evidence of basaloid nests, and the diagnosis rendered was invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. 

On April 24, he began treatment with cemiplimab 350 mg every 3 weeks. Before therapy, ^18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated a focal area of uptake in the supraorbital lesion (SUVmax 6.9; metabolic tumor volume, 2 cc). After five cycles, the plaque had regressed markedly, but several discrete papular lesions remained. Dermoscopic evaluation of these papules revealed features typical of basal cell carcinoma. A follow-up PET/CT at 12 weeks showed decreased uptake in the original lesion (SUVmax 4.8; metabolic tumor volume, 0.5 cc), consistent with partial metabolic response.

A 3-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rat was housed under standard conditions and assigned to a control group in a pharmacological study. At 7 weeks of age, the rat appeared clinically normal and was euthanized under anesthesia. At necropsy, the liver and other organs appeared grossly unremarkable, and serum AST and ALT levels were within normal limits.

A sample from the left lateral liver lobe was fixed in formalin, embedded, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin, Azan, and Watanabe’s silver stain. Histologically, there were multifocal basophilic foci located predominantly in the perilobular region. Within these foci, polygonal to short spindle-shaped cells formed small nests and sheets within dilated sinusoids without encapsulation. The tumor cells exhibited clear cell borders, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, hyperchromatic nuclei, frequent mitotic figures, and sparse hepatocellular necrosis. Narrow spaces containing erythrocytes were noted between tumor cells, and local invasion into adjacent blood vessels was seen. Azan and silver stains demonstrated reticular fibers forming a loosely connected, irregular network within tumor cell aggregates.

A 52-year-old woman was referred to endocrinology in 2011 for a 2-month history of right-sided neck swelling, worsening dysphagia, and mild pain. Her past medical history was notable for excision of a dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in the left inguinal–suprapubic region in 1998, with four local recurrences (2000, 2001, 2008, and 2009) treated surgically; she also received external radiotherapy (66 Gy) after the last excision.

On examination, there was a large, firm, mildly tender mass on the right side of the neck without fixation; the Pemberton sign was positive. Laboratory studies showed:
• TSH 0.363 mIU/L (0.32–5.0)  
• Free T4 14.6 pmol/L (9.0–19.0)  
• Anti-thyroglobulin antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Intact PTH 6 pmol/L (1.48–8.43)

Ultrasound of the thyroid revealed a right lobe volume of 50 mL and left lobe 7.3 mL; the entire right lobe was replaced by a hypo- to anechoic mass measuring approximately 6 × 4 × 6 cm, displacing the trachea 1 cm to the left, with no pathological lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the right lobe yielded a hemorrhagic background with isolated clusters of pleomorphic round and oval nuclei; it was classified as category IV/3, suspicious for primary or secondary malignancy.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and thorax confirmed a voluminous right thyroid mass and detected two pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases. MRI showed no lymphadenopathy. Laryngoscopy demonstrated freely mobile vocal cords.

A 34‐year‐old woman presented with pain and slight mobility of the mandibular right second premolar and first molar. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, percussion of both teeth was tender, and slight mobility was noted, but the overlying mucosa and skin were normal with no erythema, ulceration, or warmth. Intraoral palpation revealed bony‐hard consistency of the buccal and lingual cortices, and the mucosal integrity was intact.

An initial orthopantomogram showed a unilocular radiolucent lesion engulfing the apices of the right mandibular second premolar and a previously endodontically treated first molar, extending to the superior border of the inferior alveolar nerve canal; its irregular shape was atypical for routine periapical cysts or granulomas. Cone beam CT further demonstrated buccolingual expansion with almost complete obliteration of the lingual cortex, measuring approximately 23.4 × 14.2 × 6.6 mm.

Based on the radiographic findings, the preliminary differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, radicular cyst, and unicystic ameloblastoma.
